source: Gomes, Selman, Kautz (1998) Boosting Combinatorial Search Through Randomization (AAAI-98)
finding: A deterministic complete search is one run of a randomized search. Adding a little randomness to the branching heuristic and restarting at a cutoff removed huge run-time variance. The hardness was in the instance plus the exact heuristic, not in the instance alone.
numbers: Table 1: logistics.d (Satz) 108 min deterministic vs 95 sec randomized restarts; 3bit-adder-32 over 24 hrs vs 95 sec; 3bit-adder-31 over 24 hrs vs 165 sec; round-robin 16 over 24 hrs vs 250 sec; round-robin 18 over 48 hrs vs 1.4 hrs; round-robin 14 411 sec vs 17 min (worse).
quote: a deterministic search algorithm can be viewed as a single run of a randomized algorithm
limits: Hand-picked hard structured instances; cutoffs tuned by trial on the same instances; 1998 hardware (200MHz SGI). Round-robin 14 got slower with restarts.
agent_relevance: One long deterministic attempt is one draw from a run-time distribution. Many cheap independent attempts with different seeds can beat it by orders of magnitude when the tail is heavy.

source: Gomes, Selman, Kautz (1998) Boosting Combinatorial Search Through Randomization (AAAI-98), cutoff tables
finding: The best restart cutoff was far below the median run length. A cutoff that gives under 1 percent success per try was still best overall, because tries are cheap.
numbers: logistics.d Table 3: cutoff 4 -> success 0.00003, mean cost 147,816 backtracks; 16 -> success 0.009, mean cost 1,861 (best); 32 -> 2,405; 250 -> 13,456; 16000 -> 107,611; 128000 -> 307,550. Round-robin 16 (Table 2): best cutoff about 5e4, expected cost about 7e5 backtracks (1.4 hrs); median unrestarted run about 2e6.
limits: U-shaped cost curve: too small a cutoff (4 or less) gives near-zero success and cost explodes. The optimum needs a measured run-time profile.
agent_relevance: For an LLM agent: the best per-attempt token cap may be well below the length of a typical long attempt. Short caps with many restarts are only good if a short attempt has a non-trivial win chance.

source: Gomes, Selman, Kautz (1998) Boosting Combinatorial Search Through Randomization, formal analysis
finding: Restarting with independent seeds at fixed cutoff c is a sequence of Bernoulli trials. The total cost S is geometric, so it has finite mean and variance even if the base procedure A has infinite mean and variance. Heavy tail on the right is removed; the tail on the left is exploited.
numbers: Round-robin N=12 maximum-likelihood index of stability alpha = 0.7 (infinite mean, since alpha < 1.1 threshold used in text). N=16: some runs under 200 backtracks vs median about 2,000,000. Conjecture: left-tail alpha is below 1.0 on hard problems. N=18 solved after 20 tries of cutoff 500,000, successful run 350,632 backtracks.
limits: Analysis assumes independent runs and a known distribution. Left-tail claim is only a conjecture here.
agent_relevance: Gives the formal reason that independent restarts bound the mean cost. Needs the assumption of independence, which same-model samples only partly satisfy (guardrail G4).

source: Gomes, Selman, Kautz (1998) Boosting Combinatorial Search Through Randomization, negative case
finding: Restarts helped only where the run-time distribution was heavy-tailed. On a blocks-world planning instance no heavy tail was found and randomization gave little or no gain.
numbers: block-world.d (Satz): deterministic 30 min; randomized mean 23 min at best setting (22 hrs at another setting). Optimal equivalence parameter 30 percent; no heavy tail across cutoffs.
limits: One instance. Authors say more study is needed on what makes a problem heavy-tailed.
agent_relevance: Restart is not free gain. Before adding restarts, measure whether the attempt-length distribution has a heavy tail; if not, continuing is as good. Supports G7 (pay for itself).

source: Gomes, Selman, Crato, Kautz (2000) Heavy-Tailed Phenomena in Satisfiability and Constraint Satisfaction Problems (J. Automated Reasoning 24)
finding: Run times of randomized backtrack search on satisfiable structured instances follow Pareto-Levy power-law tails (log-log plot of survival is a straight line). Estimated indices of stability are below 1 for most cases, meaning infinite mean.
numbers: Table II (Hill-type estimate, sample k): quasigroup order 11 30pct 0.466 (k=9731); order 15 30pct 0.319 (10000); order 15 40pct 0.153; order 30 55pct 0.392; school timetabling 0.219; logistics Satz 0.360 (1442); logistics Relsat 0.670 (1000); register allocation 0.102. Runs capped at 1e6 backtracks.
limits: Tail estimated on the top 30 percent of each sample (r = 0.3k) with a cap, so tail index is approximate. Only solvable instances.
agent_relevance: Strong evidence that for search with early irreversible choices, a few attempts are extremely long. Our analogue: attempts that commit to a wrong frame early and never recover.

source: Gomes et al. (2000) Heavy-Tailed Phenomena in SAT and CSP, boundary conditions
finding: Heavy tails are absent for unsolvable instances, for local search (Walksat), and for easy instances. Stronger propagation (all-different) removes the tail for small orders because propagation alone solves them, but the tail returns at larger order. Look-back learning (Relsat) makes the tail somewhat lighter (alpha 0.670 vs 0.360 for Satz) but does not remove it.
numbers: Walksat on the logistics instance: faster-than-linear tail drop in log-log, so no heavy tail. Unsolvable quasigroup instances: best fit gamma and normal. All-different on order 30 at 55pct pre-assigned solved in under 5 min and tail reappears.
limits: Local search result is for one instance; consistent with Hoos exponential run-time claim cited there.
agent_relevance: Gives the exact conditions under which restarts pay: systematic search with early commitments on satisfiable problems. Unsatisfiable (no answer exists) cases show no benefit. For us: no gain when the task has no answer that a check could accept.

source: Gomes et al. (2000) Heavy-Tailed Phenomena in SAT and CSP, left tail and restart effect
finding: Short runs also occur far more often than a normal model predicts. Restarting with a tiny cutoff turns the distribution geometric, so failure rate falls exponentially in total work, while without restarts it falls only as a power law.
numbers: 14-team round-robin: 70pct of runs exceed 25,000 backtracks yet about 1pct finish under 650. 16-team: about 1pct under 10,000 vs median over 2,000,000. Logistics: 2pct of runs under 200 backtracks, 70pct above 100,000. Quasigroup order 20, 5pct pre-assigned: at 300 total backtracks failure about 70pct without restarts vs about 0.01pct with restart every 4 backtracks. Logistics: cutoff 16 gives about 5pct failure after 5,000 backtracks; no restarts still about 70pct failure after 100,000.
limits: Left tails shown are not formally heavy; authors only conjecture heavy left tails on very hard instances. Averages over 100 runs.
agent_relevance: Core quantitative case for many short independent tries. The analogue in sampling is pass@k rising steeply with k when single-try success is tiny but non-zero.

source: Gomes et al. (2000) Heavy-Tailed Phenomena in SAT and CSP, Table IV and prior art
finding: Randomized rapid restarts (RRR) solved several instances no backtrack solver had solved. Niemela and Bayardo-Schrag independently used restarts earlier; Bayardo-Schrag used only a fixed high cutoff.
numbers: Means over 100 runs: logistics.d 108 min vs 95 sec; 3bit-adders over 24 hrs vs 165 sec and 17 min; round-robin 14 411 sec vs 250 sec; round-robin 16 over 24 hrs vs 1.4 hrs; round-robin 18 over 48 hrs vs 22 hrs; block-world 30 min vs 23 min. Small caveat: the 16- and 18-team cutoffs were found by trial and error starting low.
limits: Cutoff for hardest instances chosen by trial and error; the 22 hrs for round-robin 18 is a mean of a handful of tries.
agent_relevance: Priority note: the idea of restarts in SAT predates the heavy-tail paper, so the novelty is the explanation and the low cutoff, not restarting itself.

source: Luby, Sinclair, Zuckerman (1993) Optimal speedup of Las Vegas algorithms (Information Processing Letters 47)
finding: With full knowledge of the run-time distribution, the optimal restart strategy is a single fixed cutoff t* repeated forever (Theorem 3). It stays optimal even when run lengths are random and runs may be suspended and resumed (Theorem 4).
numbers: Theorem 3: S_t = (t,t,t,...) minimises expected time. Remark: if p(t) = 2^(1-t) type distribution with no benefit from restart, the best is to never stop (cutoff infinite); ratio sequence tends to 3.
limits: Needs the distribution known. Assumes runs are independent and restart costs nothing beyond the lost work.
agent_relevance: Gives the clean rule: if you know the attempt-length distribution, pick one cap and repeat; never a growing schedule.

source: Luby, Sinclair, Zuckerman (1993) Optimal speedup of Las Vegas algorithms, universal strategy
finding: With zero knowledge of the distribution, the universal strategy S_univ = 1,1,2,1,1,2,4,1,1,2,1,1,2,4,8,... is within a log factor of optimal. No universal strategy can do better than a log factor. It does not even require a finite mean.
numbers: Theorem 5: T(S_univ) <= 192 * l * (log l + 5), where l = optimal expected time with known distribution. Theorem 7: lower bound of (1/8) * l * log l for any strategy over distributions with that l. Theorem 6: P(run longer than t) <= exp(-t / (64 l log t)). Authors say the constant 192 is not tuned.
limits: Worst-case guarantee over all distributions; practical constants are far better. Factor 2 growth is arbitrary, any constant ratio works.
agent_relevance: Gives a schedule when we have no profile of the task: doubling caps with each cap run twice. Use only if attempts are cheap and independent.

source: Kautz, Horvitz, Ruan, Gomes, Selman (2002) Dynamic Restart Policies (AAAI-02)
finding: Using a Bayesian decision tree on the first 10 solver choice points to predict a run as short or long, then choosing the cutoff by the prediction, beat the best fixed cutoff. Naive use of the prediction without pruning long runs did poorly.
numbers: Dynamic n-ary policy is best, then dynamic binary. Improvement over Luby's fixed optimal policy: about 40 to 65 percent in solution time on quasigroup-with-holes, graph colouring and logistics planning (CSP and Satz solvers). Knowledge-free universal Luby policy is about 6 times slower than the best dynamic policy. Observation window of 10 choice points had the best cost/benefit; leaf labelled short if over 60pct of cases short.
limits: Needs offline training on traces from the same problem family and a held-out test set. Runs assumed independent in the main analysis.
agent_relevance: An early signal in an attempt (first few steps) can predict if it will be long. In an LLM agent: a cheap early probe to cut a bad attempt, but only if trained on this task class (G1 says doubt on a signal).

source: Huang (2007) The Effect of Restarts on the Efficiency of Clause Learning (IJCAI-07)
finding: In a clause-learning SAT solver (TiniSat) every restart policy tested beat no restarts on industrial benchmarks, and Luby's universal policy (unit 32) was best overall, though no policy won on every family.
numbers: 251 industrial instances in 22 families, 2-hour cutoff. Instances solved: no restarts 127; (100,1.5) 164; (700,1) 166; (550,1) 168; (32,1.1) 174; (16000,1) 178; Luby unit 32 180; Siege 182; MiniSat 128. Total time: 11.28 days (none) vs 7.68 days (Luby). Weakest restart policy still saved 2.43 days and solved 37 more instances. On fvp-unsat-2.0 Luby was 2.5x faster than policy M vs 1.2x in aggregate.
limits: One solver, one decision heuristic (VSIDS plus BerkMin); author notes no policy is best on all families and suggests dynamic policies. Luby's optimality theorem is for Las Vegas algorithms, and learning makes runs dependent, so theory is only loosely applicable.
agent_relevance: Shows a universal restart schedule is a robust default with unknown distribution. But learning across restarts (kept state) matters: restarts in clause learning keep what was learned.

source: Huang (2007) The Effect of Restarts on the Efficiency of Clause Learning, theory of why restarts help learners
finding: Clause learning with unlimited restarts is as powerful as general resolution, while plain DPLL is exponentially weaker; a resolution proof can be simulated by learning each resolvent and restarting. So restarts in learners are not only a way to escape bad luck.
numbers: Cites Beame et al. 2004 for the proof-system result. Describes restart policy as one of the factors fixing the order of resolution steps.
limits: Theoretical simulation assumes freedom to ignore unit-propagated assignments, unlike standard practice.
agent_relevance: Restart with memory (lessons kept as no-goods) is different from restart from scratch. This links to the conflict-driven clause learning subfield; our restart should carry failed-attempt lessons, not blank state.

source: Audemard, Simon (2009) Predicting Learnt Clauses Quality in Modern SAT Solvers (IJCAI-09)
finding: Modern CDCL solvers restart so often that most restarts happen before the 1000th conflict. The meaning of restart moved from restart elsewhere in the space to reorder the variable priorities and re-enter the same space by a different path, helped by phase saving.
numbers: Statement in section 3.1: typical run has most restarts before conflict 1000; baseline MiniSat with Luby restarts starting at 100 and phase polarity.
quote: restarting was proposed as an efficient way to prevent heavy-tailed phenomena
limits: Background remark in a paper about learned-clause quality (LBD, glue clauses), not a restart study itself.
agent_relevance: Practice drifted from restart-to-escape-luck to restart-with-saved-state. For an agent: a restart that keeps good partial work (saved phase) behaves differently from one that starts blank.

source: Gomes, Selman (1997) Algorithm Portfolio Design: Theory vs. Practice (UAI-97)
finding: Treat a portfolio as a random variable (min over processors of run time). Mean and standard deviation (risk) of the portfolio are computed from each algorithm's cumulative distribution. The best mix shifts with the number of processors.
numbers: Quasigroup order 20, 10,000 runs per strategy. Brelaz-S dominates the early part of the distribution, R-Brelaz-R the later part. With 2 processors: two copies of R-Brelaz-R best in mean and risk. With 5 processors the efficient set had three portfolios (0, 1 or 2 Brelaz-S). With 20 processors all-Brelaz-S was best in mean and standard deviation.
limits: Single problem family; portfolio computed assuming independent runs and no communication.
agent_relevance: With more parallel budget, shift toward high-variance, fast-when-lucky attempt types. With little budget, pick the low-variance one. Fits G12 (spend by budget).

source: Gomes, Selman (1997) Algorithm Portfolio Design: Theory vs. Practice, conclusions
finding: Counter-intuitive result: even when neither of two stochastic algorithms dominates, running many copies of the single better one can beat a mixed portfolio. Random restarts of a good stochastic method are often close to the optimal strategy.
numbers: Compare Figures 8 and 10 in the paper (2 and 20 processors).
quote: running multiple copies of a single algorithm is preferrable to a mix of algorithms
limits: Holds in the quasigroup setting studied; the authors note the portfolio value depends on how distributions cross.
agent_relevance: Argues against persona or strategy mixing in favour of plain repeated sampling, matching our guardrail G4.

source: Zilberstein (1996) Using Anytime Algorithms in Intelligent Systems (AI Magazine 17(3))
finding: Anytime algorithms trade deliberation time for result quality and can be stopped at any point with a usable answer. The article surveys control of systems built from several anytime algorithms, in signal interpretation, real-time diagnosis and robot control. Only the abstract page could be read this session.
numbers: AI Magazine vol 17 issue 3 (Fall 1996), p. 73. Standard properties from memory (not verified here): measurable quality, recognisable quality, monotonicity, consistency, diminishing returns, interruptibility.
limits: Abstract only; full PDF download returned empty. Property list is from memory.
agent_relevance: Gives the vocabulary for guardrail G6: always hold a best answer so far, and track a performance profile of quality against time.

source: Dean, Boddy (1988) An analysis of time-dependent planning (AAAI-88)
finding: From memory: introduced time-dependent planning and performance profiles (expected answer quality as a function of time) and showed how to allocate time between deliberation and action. Cited as the origin of anytime algorithms in the Gomes-Selman paper.
numbers: none recorded
limits: Not opened this session. Cited in the opened UAI-97 paper as the origin of anytime algorithms.
agent_relevance: The idea that each operator or step has a measurable quality-versus-time curve and a controller allocates time. Basis for budgeted scaffold decisions.

source: Korf (1985) Depth-first iterative-deepening: an optimal admissible tree search (Artificial Intelligence 27)
finding: From memory: iterative deepening repeats depth-limited search with a growing bound. In trees with a growing branching factor it costs only a constant factor more than breadth-first, while using memory linear in depth, and is asymptotically optimal among brute-force admissible searches. Not opened (the PDF download failed).
numbers: none verified
limits: From memory only.
agent_relevance: Iterative deepening is the schedule cousin of Luby: restart with a growing bound. The overhead is small when cost grows geometrically with depth.

source: Luby, Sinclair, Zuckerman (1993) Optimal speedup of Las Vegas algorithms, interpretation of the restart-or-continue question
finding: Whether to restart or continue depends only on the shape of the run-time distribution. If hazard rate of finishing falls over time (heavy tail), restart. If it rises or is constant, continuing is as good or better. The paper notes that for some distributions continuing the first run beats any restart.
numbers: Remark in section 2: example distribution p(t) = 2^(1-t) for t > 1 has ratio sequence decreasing to 3, so it is always better to continue the first run than stop.
limits: Pure Las Vegas setting: answer is checkable and runs are independent.
agent_relevance: A direct decision rule for a restart operator: estimate whether the chance of finishing per extra token falls as an attempt gets longer. If it falls, restart; if not, continue.

source: Truchet, Richoux, Codognet (2013) Prediction of Parallel Speed-ups for Las Vegas Algorithms (ICPP)
finding: Parallel speed-up of independent multi-walk runs is determined by the order statistic (minimum) of the sequential run-time distribution. A pure exponential gives linear speed-up. A shifted exponential or lognormal has a finite speed-up limit as cores grow.
numbers: Costas array problem with Adaptive Search: linear or better speed-up up to 256 cores, near-linear far beyond. Predictions fitted from about 650 sequential run times per benchmark.
limits: Local-search style solvers and CSP benchmarks; assumes independent walks with no communication.
agent_relevance: Predicts how much running N independent LLM attempts in parallel can gain: look at the left tail of the single-attempt latency or success distribution. A minimum start cost (shift) caps the gain.

source: Brown, Juravsky, Ehrlich, Clark, Le, Re, Mirhoseini (2024) Large Language Monkeys: Scaling Inference Compute with Repeated Sampling
finding: For LLMs, independent restarts are repeated samples. Coverage (share of problems with at least one correct sample) grows nearly log-linearly with sample count over four orders of magnitude, and fits an exponentiated power law.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite with DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Instruct: 15.9pct with 1 sample to 56pct with 250 samples. CodeContests with Gemma-2B: 0.02pct with 1 sample to 7.1pct with 10,000 samples (over 300x). MATH with Llama-3-8B-Instruct coverage rises from 82.9pct at 1 sample.
limits: Gains count only where an automatic verifier can pick the right sample; without a verifier majority vote and reward models plateau. Coverage, not final accuracy.
agent_relevance: Direct LLM analogue of heavy-tailed restart gain: tiny single-try success can be turned into large coverage by many independent tries. Needs a code-run check (G3, G5).

source: Snell, Lee, Xu, Kumar (2024) Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters
finding: Continuing (sequential revisions of one answer) is better on easy questions; restarting (independent parallel samples) or tree search is better on hard questions that need a different high-level approach. Choosing per question difficulty gives about 4x less compute than best-of-N.
numbers: Compute-optimal allocation beats best-of-N using about 4x less computation for revisions and search. FLOPs-matched: test-time compute on a smaller model can beat a 14x larger model on easy and intermediate questions. Revision model: about 38pct of correct answers flipped to incorrect by naive revision. Equal-budget test with a verifier or majority selection: sequential revisions narrowly beat parallel for the revision model on MATH.
limits: MATH with PaLM-2 variants, fine-tuned revision model and trained verifier (PRM/ORM); results depend on those. Difficulty bins from model's own pass rate.
agent_relevance: Gives the LLM version of restart vs continue: easy items continue and revise; hard items restart. Matches G12. The 38pct flip-back rate warns that continuing can destroy a correct answer.

source: Gomes et al. (2000) and Gomes et al. (1998), shared lesson on instance and algorithm interaction
finding: The earlier finding of exceptionally hard problems in fixed distributions (Gent and Walsh; Smith and Grant) was reinterpreted: hardness was in the pairing of instance and a deterministic heuristic. Changing random seeds made the same instance easy on some runs.
numbers: Same instance, many seeds gave the same heavy-tailed shape as seen across a collection of instances.
limits: Explained with Gent-Walsh and Smith-Grant as secondary citations; the original phase-transition papers were not opened.
agent_relevance: A prompt that makes the model fail repeatedly on a case may fail through its framing; a changed seed or reframing can solve it. Supports the S2 reframe operator.

source: Gomes, Selman, Kautz (1998) Boosting Combinatorial Search Through Randomization, how the cutoff is found
finding: When the full distribution cannot be measured (instances too hard), the authors use trial and error on cutoffs starting low, because the optimum sits below the median. This is an informal unknown-distribution search that Luby universal later formalises.
numbers: Round-robin 16: cutoff 1,000,000 gave under 40pct success (below median), each run about 2 hours. Final cutoff about 5e4 to 5e5 depending on N.
limits: No guarantee; heuristics learned on the specific instance.
agent_relevance: Practical rule: start with small caps and only grow if nothing succeeds, which is the Luby idea in spirit.

source: Kautz et al. (2002) Dynamic Restart Policies, background on policy classes
finding: Summarises three classes of restart policy: knowing nothing but run length (Luby universal), knowing the full distribution (fixed optimal cutoff), and using observations of the current run (dynamic). Notes that for a mixed ensemble of easy and hard instances no single fixed cutoff is optimal, and portfolios can lower mean and variance even if each member has high mean and variance.
numbers: Qualitative; example in the text shows with a mixed distribution a fixed cutoff below 100 gives a finite chance of never solving the hard class.
limits: Review part of a primary paper; relies on citations to Gomes and Selman 2001 which was not opened.
agent_relevance: Name the three states of knowledge for an agent: no profile, a profile, a live signal. Choose the schedule to match.

source: Gomes, Selman (2001) Algorithm portfolios (Artificial Intelligence 126)
finding: Extended the portfolio work. Search result and citing paper state it shows that a high-variance (risk-seeking) strategy can be advantageous in a portfolio, and that portfolios can have low mean and low variance even when members have high mean and variance. Full PDF was downloaded but its text could not be extracted this session.
numbers: none verified
limits: Not read in full. Claims taken from the abstract in a search snippet and from the Kautz 2002 introduction.
agent_relevance: Same as a15: with spare parallel budget prefer risky fast attempts.

source: Huberman, Lukose, Hogg (1997) An economics approach to hard computational problems (Science 275)
finding: From memory and citation: first to frame portfolio of algorithms using mean-variance (risk) trade-off from finance, with experiments showing speed-up when running a heavy-tailed algorithm in parallel with others. Cited in the opened UAI-97 and AAAI-02 papers as the origin of portfolios. The paper text was not opened.
numbers: none verified
limits: Not opened; the Science reference in the UAI-97 list prints 265, which looks like an error for 275.
agent_relevance: Source of the risk-return view of attempts.
